d: Task Scheduler coordinates tasks done in each frame as the game runs.
h:
The task scheduler coordinates tasks done each frame as the game runs, even when it is paused. These tasks include detecting player input, animating characters, updating the physics simulation, and resuming scripts in a task.wait() state.

While there may be multiple tasks running, the task scheduler can potentially be overloaded, especially in the following situations:

  • Using a custom character rig or input scheme.
  • Animating parts yourself (instead of using an Animator).
  • Depending heavily on precise physics.
  • Replicating objects regularly.

RunService

The most direct way to add frame-by-frame tasks is through the following members of RunService:

  • RunService.PreAnimation
  • RunService.PreSimulation
  • RunService.PostSimulation
  • RunService.Heartbeat
  • RunService:BindToRenderStep()
  • RunService.PreRender

Scheduler priority

The task scheduler categorizes and completes tasks in the following order. Some tasks may not perform work in a frame, while others may run multiple times.

* Script execution during RunService.Heartbeat differs depending on your game's Workspace.SignalBehavior setting. See Deferred events.

Best practices

To build performant games with efficiency in mind, note the following:

  • Don't connect/bind functions to the render step unless absolutely necessary. Only tasks that must be done after input but before rendering should be done in such a way, like camera movement. For strict control over order, use BindToRenderStep() instead of PreRender.

  • Manage physical states carefully. PreSimulation happens before physics, while PostSimulation happens after physics. Therefore, gameplay logic that affects the physics state should be done in PreSimulation, such as setting the Velocity of parts. In contrast, gameplay logic that relies on or reacts to the physics state should be handled in PostSimulation, such as reading the Position of parts to detect when they enter defined zones.

  • Motor6D transform changes should be done on the PreSimulation event. If you don't, Animators will overwrite changes on the next frame. Even without an Animator, PreSimulation is the last Luau event fired before Motor6D.Transform is applied to part positions.

kid.simple: Every frame, Roblox has a to-do list: read player input, animate characters, run physics, resume waiting scripts, and draw the screen. The task scheduler is what runs that list in order. Knowing the order helps you hook your code into the right moment, like before physics or after physics. Too much per-frame code can overload the scheduler and make the game stutter.
kid.analogy: It is like a school day schedule: homeroom, math, lunch, gym. If you want to change your gym clothes, you do it right before gym, not after.
keyPoints: The task scheduler runs each frame's jobs, like input, animation, physics, and resuming scripts paused with `task.wait()`.
It can get overloaded by custom character rigs, animating parts yourself instead of using an `Animator`, heavy physics, and replicating objects a lot.
Only use render step hooks for things that must happen after input but before drawing, like camera movement.
Use `BindToRenderStep()` instead of `PreRender` when you need strict control over order.
Change physics stuff (like a part's velocity) in `PreSimulation`, which runs before physics.
Read physics results (like a part's position) in `PostSimulation`, which runs after physics.
Change `Motor6D.Transform` in `PreSimulation`, or the `Animator` will overwrite it.

terms.task scheduler: The part of Roblox that runs all of a frame's jobs in a set order.
terms.frame: One update of the game. At 60 FPS there are 60 frames each second.
terms.RunService: A service with events that fire at certain moments every frame.
terms.render step: The moment just before the screen is drawn. Code here delays drawing, so keep it tiny.
terms.simulation: The physics step, where Roblox moves falling, bouncing, and pushed parts.
terms.PreSimulation: Fires every frame right before physics runs. Good for pushing things.
terms.PostSimulation: Fires every frame right after physics runs. Good for checking where things ended up.
terms.velocity: How fast and in what direction something moves. A velocity of (0, 50, 0) moves a part up 50 studs per second.
terms.Motor6D: A joint that connects two body parts, like an arm to a torso, and can rotate them for animation.
terms.rig: The set of parts and joints that make up a character's body.

example.title: Detect when a ball enters a goal zone
example.place: Script in ServerScriptService (with a part named Ball and a part named GoalZone in Workspace)
example.code:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local ball = Workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")
local goalZone = Workspace:WaitForChild("GoalZone")

local scored = false

-- PostSimulation runs right after physics, so the ball's position is up to date
RunService.PostSimulation:Connect(function()
	if scored then
		return
	end

	-- Is the ball inside the goal zone's box?
	local localPos = goalZone.CFrame:PointToObjectSpace(ball.Position)
	local half = goalZone.Size / 2
	if math.abs(localPos.X) <= half.X
		and math.abs(localPos.Y) <= half.Y
		and math.abs(localPos.Z) <= half.Z then
		scored = true
		print("Goal!")
	end
end)
explain: We find the ball and the goal zone in the Workspace.
We connect to `PostSimulation`, which fires every frame right after physics moved the ball.
`PointToObjectSpace` tells us where the ball is measured from the goal zone's center. If the zone is 10 studs wide, the ball is inside when its X is between -5 and 5.
If the ball is inside on all three axes, we print Goal! once.
Reading the position after physics means we always check where the ball really is this frame.

watchOut: Putting lots of code in render step hooks. That delays drawing every frame. Only use them for things like the camera.
Setting a part's speed in `PostSimulation`. Physics already ran, so the change waits a frame. Use `PreSimulation`.
Changing `Motor6D.Transform` outside `PreSimulation`. The `Animator` will overwrite it next frame.
Animating parts by hand every frame when an `Animator` could do it. This adds load to the task scheduler.
